The Chatham petrel Pterodroma axillaris is a medium-sized gadfly petrel endemic to the Chatham Islands of New Zealand, where it nests exclusively in burrows dug within the soft peat soils of remnant coastal forest and scrub. Breeding is highly seasonal, with adults returning to their natal colonies in the austral spring to engage in courtship displays and nest-site preparation. Field studies of marked individuals indicate that a single egg constitutes the annual reproductive output, a life-history trait typical of many Procellariiformes. Females produce exactly one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch], and they do so only once per breeding season, resulting in approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. When maintained under typical active metabolic conditions equivalent to a body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], the calculated maximum reproductive rate is thus one offspring per 365 days, a figure that aligns well with the slow, K-selected life-history strategy of this threatened seabird. Conspecific comparisons with other Pterodroma species confirm this minimal reproductive output, reflecting the intense energetic demands of long-distance foraging trips across the open ocean.

Newly hatched chicks of the Chatham petrel emerge from their calcareous egg with a modest weight that reflects the limited yolk reserves available at the point of hatching. The mean wet weight at birth has been documented at 45 grams [Wwb = 45 grams], a value consistent with the neonatal masses reported for other gadfly petrels of comparable adult body size. This initial mass is relatively low compared to the adult asymptotic mass, and it underscores the high degree of parental investment required during the nestling period. The chicks, which are semi-precocial and brooded intensively for their first week of life, are entirely dependent on the regurgitated meals brought by both parents. The relatively small wet weight of the neonate is thought to be an adaptation linked to the energetic constraints of egg production in a bird that lays only a single egg annually, allowing the female to allocate resources efficiently during the pre-laying period without exceeding local foraging capacity.

Throughout the nestling phase, the developing chick grows rapidly, achieving a substantial increase in body mass before it is ready to fledge. Long-term growth monitoring studies have revealed that the maximum recorded asymptotic mass attained by a nestling Chatham petrel is 630 grams [Wwi = 630 grams], a value that represents the ultimate wet weight reached prior to the pre-fledging mass recession that occurs in many procellariiform species. This peak mass is attained during the late nestling stage, after which the chick may lose some weight as it metabolizes stored fat reserves and undergoes physiological preparation for life at sea. The developmental schedule leading to this asymptotic mass is tightly regulated by parental provisioning frequency and the energy density of the diet, which consists primarily of small fish, squid, and crustaceans. The size of the nestling at this asymptotic stage is comparable to or even slightly exceeds the body mass of the average adult breeding bird, a common pattern among seabirds that build substantial lipid reserves to buffer against irregular feeding visits.

The temporal progression of development in the Chatham petrel follows a predictable sequence under stable thermal conditions. At a mean incubation temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], incubation of the single egg requires approximately 47 days [ab = approximately 47 days], a duration that is typical for an altricial seabird that must develop a well-organized neural and thermoregulatory system before hatching. This period is followed by an extended nestling phase that culminates in fledging. Once the chick has completed its growth and reached the appropriate developmental stage, it departs the burrow permanently. Sexual maturation and the onset of reproductive activity are delayed considerably in this long-lived seabird, as is characteristic of Procellariiformes.
